---
title: "LoRA Optimizations"
description: "Custom autograd functions and Triton kernels in Axolotl for optimized LoRA fine-tuning"
---

Inspired by [Unsloth](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth), we've implemented two
optimizations for LoRA and QLoRA fine-tuning, supporting both single GPU and multi-GPU
(including the DDP, DeepSpeed, and FSDP2 settings) training. These include (1) SwiGLU
and GEGLU activation function Triton kernels, and (2) LoRA MLP and attention custom
autograd functions. Our goal was to leverage operator fusion and tensor re-use in order
to improve speed and reduce memory usage during the forward and backward passes of
these calculations.

We currently support several common model architectures, including (but not limited to):

- `llama`
- `mistral`
- `qwen2`
- `gemma`
- `gemma2`
- `gemma3`

<details>

The set of models we support is currently limited by our attention patching strategy,
which assumes (and replaces) specific code blocks for query / key / value and output
projections:

```python
ORIGINAL_QKV_CODE = """
    query_states = self.q_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
    key_states = self.k_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
    value_states = self.v_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
""".lstrip(
    "\n"
)

ORIGINAL_O_CODE = """
    attn_output = self.o_proj(attn_output)
""".lstrip(
    "\n"
)
```

Is replaced with:

```python
PATCHED_QKV_CODE = """
    query_states, key_states, value_states = self.apply_qkv(hidden_states)
    query_states = query_states.view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
    key_states = key_states.view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
    value_states = value_states.view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)
""".lstrip(
    "\n"
)

PATCHED_O_CODE = """
    attn_output = self.apply_o(attn_output)
""".lstrip(
    "\n"
)
```

Where `apply_qkv` and `apply_o` are defined in the `axolotl.kernels.lora` module.

We welcome testing of other model architectures and / or PRs to expand our patching
logic to be compatible with more of them.

</details>

::: {.callout-tip}
Check out our [LoRA optimizations blog](https://axolotlai.substack.com/p/accelerating-lora-fine-tuning-with).
:::

## Usage

These optimizations can be enabled in your Axolotl config YAML file. The
`lora_mlp_kernel` option enables the optimized MLP path, while `lora_qkv_kernel` and
`lora_o_kernel` enable the fused query-key-value projection and optimized output
projection, respectively.

```yaml
lora_mlp_kernel: true
lora_qkv_kernel: true
lora_o_kernel: true
```

::: {.callout-note}
Currently, LoRA kernels are not supported for RLHF training, only SFT.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
LoRA kernels do not support remote modeling code.
:::

## Requirements

- One or more NVIDIA or AMD GPUs (in order to use the Triton kernels)
    - Note: Set `TORCH_ROCM_AOTRITON_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL=1` to enable [memory-efficient attention on AMD GPUs](https://github.com/ROCm/aotriton/issues/16#issuecomment-2346675491)
- Targeted LoRA adapters cannot use Dropout
    - This may limit model expressivity / cause overfitting
- Targeted LoRA adapters cannot have bias terms
    - This may limit model expressivity

Models with pre-existing LoRA adapters that use Dropout or have bias terms may need to
be re-finetuned without these features in order to be useful.

## Implementation details

### Custom autograd functions

The LoRA MLP autograd function optimizes the entire MLP computation path. It fuses the
LoRA and base weight computations together and provides a single, efficient backward
pass for the entire MLP block.

For attention components, similar optimizations are provided through a function that
handles the query, key, and value projections, and a function that handles the output
projection. They are designed to work with the existing `transformers` attention
implementation via some monkey-patching logic.

### Triton kernels

Two activation functions (SwiGLU and GeGLU) are implemented with Triton kernels for
improved speed and memory performance. These kernels handle both the forward and
backward passes.

### Integration

The custom autograd functions and Triton kernels are designed to work together. The
autograd function manages the high-level computation flow and gradient tracking, while
calling the Triton kernels for the activation function computation. During the backward
pass, the kernel computes both the activation output and the required gradients, which
the autograd function then uses to compute the final gradients for the entire
computation path.

## Future Work

- Support for additional model architectures
- Support for dropout and bias
- Additional operator fusions


## FP32 LoRA gradients

```yaml
adapter: lora  # also supported with qlora
bf16: true
lora_fp32_gradients: true
```

On single-device, DDP, and FSDP2 training, this opt-in setting keeps trainable LoRA
parameters and their accumulated gradients in FP32. PyTorch requires a parameter
and its `.grad` to have the same dtype. DeepSpeed instead uses native FP32 master
gradients and accumulation buffers, described below.
Frozen base weights and unrelated trainable tensors retain their existing dtype.
It applies to newly initialized and loaded adapters, overrides adapter downcasting,
and defaults to `false` so existing parameter-storage choices stay unchanged.

Dense fused QKV, QK, output, gated-MLP, and GatedDeltaNet projection kernels now
retain FP32 parameter-gradient reduction outputs whenever their original LoRA
parameters are FP32, including adapters already upcast by PEFT. CUDA uses BF16/FP16
GEMM inputs with FP32 outputs, avoiding full-size FP32 activation copies. Embedding
backward already accumulates in FP32. Low-rank intermediates, activation derivatives,
and forward outputs still use their compute dtype; this reduces rounding but does
not make fused and unfused implementations bit-identical. Merge-aware NVFP4
projections continue through their protected forward to preserve fake quantization.
Native weight-only torchao `NVFP4Tensor` base layers retain their quantized forward/autograd,
while adapter output addition and input/A/B gradients use a custom LoRA delta
function. Dense SwiGLU/GEGLU activations use fused forward/backward kernels.
Nemotron-H dense/shared ReLU² MLPs use optimized up/down LoRA projections and a
fused ReLU² activation derivative. Routed 3D expert tensors stay with their MoE
backend; these dense kernels do not optimize routed experts.

The setting supports single-device/DDP, FSDP2, and DeepSpeed ZeRO. For FSDP2,
Axolotl preserves the loaded parameter dtypes (`param_dtype: null`) and selects
FP32 gradient reduction (`reduce_dtype: float32`). Frozen base weights remain in
their loaded precision; LoRA parameters stay FP32 through unsharding. Normal BF16
training/autocast still applies to compute operations.

For DeepSpeed, Axolotl sets `data_types.grad_accum_dtype: fp32` and
`communication_data_type: fp32`, disables FP16/BF16 master gradients and BF16 optimizer states,
and enables immediate BF16 gradient-buffer updates. These settings override
conflicting values in the supplied DeepSpeed config via a generated copy; the
original JSON file is unchanged. DeepSpeed can retain BF16 working parameters and
per-microbatch gradients while its master gradients and accumulation buffers are
FP32. The fused per-microbatch reduction therefore still follows working-parameter
precision on that backend. Use ZeRO stages 1–3 for BF16 DeepSpeed training; stage 0
with BF16 working parameters and FP32 accumulation is unsupported by DeepSpeed.
Gradient communication precision applies to all trainable tensors in the backend.
Axolotl also preserves FP32 reduction and partition buffers in ZeRO-2/3 and
converts each ZeRO-2 microbatch gradient before summing. Some DeepSpeed versions
otherwise round reduced gradients back to the working-parameter dtype or apply
the requested dtype only after accumulation. FP32 reduction buckets and partition
buffers use twice the memory of BF16 buffers; ZeRO-2 overlapping communication
uses two reduction buckets. Working model parameters keep their original dtype.
ZeRO-1/2 **optimizer offload is rejected** with this option: its separate offload
path still accumulates in the working-parameter dtype. Disable optimizer offload
or use ZeRO-3; ZeRO-3 offload has not been validated here.

For BF16 LoRA weights, FP32 adds two bytes per parameter for weights and another
two for gradients. Qwen3-8B rank 16 on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down has 43,646,976 adapter
parameters: about 167 MiB extra for weights plus gradients per adapter. Optimizers
that keep moments in parameter dtype, such as ordinary AdamW, can add another
167 MiB for their two moments; other optimizers differ. PEFT may already keep these
tensors in FP32, in which case there is no additional persistent allocation.

Use the same setting when resuming an exact experiment. Single-device/DDP/FSDP2 adapter checkpoints contain
FP32 weights; DeepSpeed exports may retain the working-parameter dtype. The YAML
controls loading/training precision. Multi-LoRA honors
this top-level option for adapter storage and its independent accumulation windows;
its separate buffer-only option does not promote adapter weights.

Dynamic NVFP4 activation quantization is rejected by the LoRA kernel path because
torchao's activation conversion does not retain the base input gradient. Use
weight-only NVFP4 bases for training with these kernels.
